correctness.rationale: A greedy subsequence embedding is earliest at each step in any prefix of a q-periodic permutation word. For each palindrome, reflected opposite transitions contribute exactly q unless an adjacent half-word pair agrees, when the contribution is 2q; even length adds a central q. Thus the greedy final index is v_1+q(m+e). Comparing with kq+s proves precisely m+e<k or m+e=k with v_1<s, including all k=1,s=0 boundary cases. The q-ary half-word transition count gives the exact binomial length spectrum; independent formal geometric summation gives both rational terms. The shipped verify.py generated 49 literal host cases with 3086 distinct palindromes, 67121 palindrome membership comparisons, and 50932 formal coefficient comparisons. These checks supplement, but do not replace, the proof.

originality.rationale: The leading 2021 primary study supplies general or extremal bounds but no exact counting of all lengths for powers of a q-ary cyclic permutation and partial final prefixes. The 2019 circular-word study concerns longest subsequence existence rather than distinct-palindrome counts. A pre-existing result for binary alternating prefixes (q=2) is explicitly outside the claim; the new theorem covers q>=3 with an alphabet-dependent half-word classification and exact endpoint-boundary correction for all s. Relevant source statements and implications were compared; unlocated specialized equivalents remain a residual risk.
residual_risks: An unlocated specialized q-ary periodic-word publication could have an equivalent or stronger result.
No claim of priority is established by a bounded literature and research-record search.
Binary case is already known and is excluded; current value rests on the complete nonbinary family and incomplete-period exact classification.

value.rationale: Scattered-palindrome complexity is a standard exact word invariant with general bounds but comparatively few tractable structured all-length families. Here all q>=3, k, and s are settled together, with a one-statistic membership theorem, rational length distribution, sharp longest length, and the invariant increment produced by appending one symbol of the incomplete final period. Unlike an arbitrary small enumeration, these solve a motivated complete family and give explicit benchmark distributions for subsequence enumeration and extremal comparisons.
